1 Executive summary

Our client sells BBQ sauce and wants to know how many bottles it will sell over the next 30 days, so that it can plan production and stock. We received five and a half years of daily sales together with daily weather data for Germany. Our job was to build a complete forecasting workflow, from cleaning the data to a final forecast, and to find out whether the weather actually helps to predict sales.

The short version of what we found is below. Every number is explained in detail in the following chapters.

2 The business problem and the data

2.1 Why a 30-day forecast?

BBQ sauce is a seasonal product. The company has to decide weeks in advance how much to produce and how much to ship to retailers. If it produces too little, shelves are empty in the main season. If it produces too much, bottles sit in the warehouse. A reliable estimate of the total amount for the next month is therefore more useful to the business than a perfect prediction of every single day.

This is also why we judge our models mainly on how well they predict the 30-day total, not only on daily errors.

2.2 The two data sets

File Content Period
bbq_sauce_sales.csv number of bottles sold per day Jan 2021 to Jul 2026
climate_data_2026.csv daily Germany-wide temperature, rain and sunshine (mean, minimum and maximum over all weather stations), from the German Weather Service (DWD) same period

The weather file has nine columns: for each of temperature (°C), precipitation (mm) and sunshine (hours) it gives the national mean, the lowest station value and the highest station value.

After loading, the sales file has 1,385 rows and the weather file 1,386 rows. The data run from 03 January 2021 to 29 July 2026.

2.3 Data preparation

Before any model can be trained, the data needs to be a clean, continuous daily series. We made four decisions:

  1. One date appears twice in the weather file, with slightly different values. We cannot tell which row is correct, so we took the average of the two.
  2. Days without any sales record. The sales file only contains days on which the company recorded sales. Forecasting tools need one row for every calendar day, so we added the missing days and set their sales to 0. Almost all of them are Mondays, Sundays and public holidays, which fits the idea that nothing was shipped on those days.
  3. Weather gaps that appeared through step 2 were filled by linear interpolation between the neighbouring days.
  4. Very large orders are kept. Some days show several thousand bottles. These are real sales (most likely large orders from retailers), so removing them would make the forecast too low. Instead we use models and error measures that can deal with such spikes.
Value
Calendar days in the clean series 2,034
Days without a sales record (set to 0) 649
Days with 0 bottles in total 38%
Median bottles per day 38
Average bottles per day 329
Largest day 5,703 bottles

The gap between the median day (38 bottles) and the average day (329 bottles) already tells an important story: on a normal day only a few bottles are sold, but a small number of very large orders pull the average up. The 10% biggest days alone account for 68% of all bottles sold.

3 Exploring the sales

Before building models we looked at the data from several angles. The goal was to understand which patterns a model could learn: trends, seasons, weekly rhythms and the role of the weather.

3.1 Sales over time

How to read it. The top panel shows every single day. The bottom panel adds up each week (grey area) and smooths it with an 8-week moving average (red line), which makes the bigger movements easier to see.

What we see. The daily line looks almost like random spikes: most days are low, and every few days a big order shoots up to 2,000 to 5,000 bottles. This is the main difficulty of the project. On the weekly level a clear pattern appears. Every year the red line rises in late winter, peaks in spring and early summer and falls again in autumn. We also see that 2024 and 2025 were stronger years than 2022 and 2023, so the level of sales is not constant over time.

3.2 Seasonality: months and weekdays

How to read it. Left: the average monthly total over all years. The main season (March to June) is highlighted in red. Right: the average number of bottles on each day of the week.

What we see. The strongest month is Mar with about 16,250 bottles, roughly 3.0 times the weakest month, Dec. Interestingly, the peak comes before the hottest months of July and August. This makes sense for a product that retailers stock up on before the BBQ season starts. On the weekly level the pattern is very sharp: there are no sales on Mondays at all, very few on Sundays, and the business happens from Tuesday to Saturday. A good model must know the day of the week.

3.3 Year-by-year comparison

How to read it. Each cell is one month of one year. Darker blue means more bottles. Empty cells at the end of 2026 are months that have not happened yet.

What we see. The spring season is visible in every year, but its size changes a lot. For example, March 2021 and March 2022 were very strong, while 2023 was a weaker year overall (90,099 bottles compared to 138,307 in 2024). Single months can also jump because of one or two very big orders. This variation is the reason why we later give our forecast as a range and not only as one number.

3.4 How sales are distributed

How to read it. Left: how often a day of a certain size occurs. Because the values range from 1 to over 5,000 bottles, the axis uses a log scale. Right: we sort all days from biggest to smallest and add them up. The dashed lines mark the top 10% of days.

What we see. There are two groups of days: many small days with tens to a few hundred bottles, and a separate group of large orders above 1,000 bottles. The right chart shows how much depends on these large orders: the top 10% of days bring 68% of all bottles. For the forecast this means that predicting when exactly a big order arrives is very hard, but predicting how many bottles arrive over a month is much more realistic.

3.5 Does the weather matter?

  correlation (daily) correlation (weekly)
mean temp 0.04 0.08
min temp 0.04 0.09
max temp 0.04 0.09
mean precipitation -0.10 -0.01
min precipitation -0.09 -0.04
max precipitation -0.08 -0.01
mean sun hours 0.06 0.25
min sun hours -0.00 0.27
max sun hours 0.06 0.23
How to read it. Each dot is one week: its average weather on the horizontal axis and the bottles sold that week on the vertical axis. The black line is a simple trend. The table shows the Spearman rank correlation, which goes from -1 (opposite movement) to +1 (same movement) and is robust to the large outliers in our data.

What we see. Day by day, the weather is almost unrelated to sales: all daily correlations are close to zero. On the weekly level, sunshine shows a moderate positive relation (ρ = 0.25), while temperature is much weaker (ρ = 0.08) and rain has practically no effect. We have to be careful with this result, because sunny weeks and the spring sales season happen at the same time of year. The sunshine relation could therefore just be the season in disguise. Whether the weather adds anything beyond the season is one of the questions our models answer in chapter 6.

4 Our forecasting approach

4.1 Splitting the data in time

With time series we can never mix up the order of the data. A model may only learn from the past and is then checked on the future, exactly as it would be used in practice. We split the series into three parts:

Part Period Days Used for
Training 03 Jan 2021 to 03 Aug 2025 1674 learning the patterns
Validation 04 Aug 2025 to 30 Jan 2026 180 choosing settings and features
Test 31 Jan 2026 to 29 Jul 2026 180 final, honest check (used only once)

Both the validation and the test period are 180 days long, which is exactly six windows of 30 days. That way we test the model six times on the same task it will have in reality: forecasting the next 30 days.

4.2 Features: what the model looks at

A machine learning model cannot work with a date directly. We have to turn the history into numbers that describe the situation on each day. We built five groups of features:

Group Features Why we use them
Lags sales 1 to 7, 14, 21 and 28 days ago (optionally 364 days, the same weekday last year) recent level and the weekly rhythm
Rolling windows mean and standard deviation of the last 7 and 28 days recent trend and how volatile sales currently are
Calendar day of the week, and day of the year and month as sine and cosine waves weekly and yearly seasonality; the sine/cosine form tells the model that December and January are neighbours
Holidays German public holidays, the day before a holiday, days until Easter or Ascension Day (Father’s Day) BBQ occasions and days when shops are closed
Weather the nine DWD values plus 7-day averages of temperature, rain and sunshine possible effect of the weather on demand

In total the model can use 26 external features (14 calendar and holiday features, 12 weather features) plus the lag and rolling-window features of past sales.

NoteThe weather of the future is unknown

When we forecast the next 30 days, we do not know the weather on those days. Using the real weather would be cheating. For the future we therefore use the long-term average weather for each day of the year (called “climatology”). This is what a forecaster in the real world would have available.

4.3 Benchmarks and how we measure errors

A model is only useful if it beats simple rules that need no machine learning at all. We compare every model with two such baselines:

  • Seasonal naive: sales on the same weekday one year earlier.
  • Weekday average: the average of each weekday over the last 8 weeks.

We measure the error in four ways:

Measure Meaning
MAE average daily error in bottles
RMSE like MAE, but large misses count more
WAPE total absolute error divided by total sales
30-day total error average error of the sum over each 30-day window, in % — this is the number the business cares about most

We did not use MAPE (the percentage error per day), because many days have zero sales and the measure would divide by zero.

5 Building and tuning the models

5.1 Which models?

We tested two tree-based models. Tree models are a good fit here because they can handle the many zero days and sudden spikes without assuming a straight-line relationship.

  • LightGBM with a Tweedie loss. LightGBM builds many small decision trees one after the other, where each tree corrects the mistakes of the previous ones. The Tweedie loss is a setting made for exactly our type of data: counts with many zeros and a few very large values.
  • Random Forest. Many independent decision trees, each trained on a random part of the data, whose predictions are averaged.

Both are used inside a recursive forecaster (from the skforecast library): the model predicts tomorrow, then uses that prediction as an input to predict the day after, and so on for 30 days.

5.2 Hyperparameter tuning

Each model has settings (hyperparameters) such as the number of trees or how deep each tree may grow. We also had to decide how many past days the model should look at. We tried every combination on a grid and judged each one on the validation period, using WAPE + 30-day total error as the score.

How to read it. Every point is one combination of settings, sorted from best (left) to worst (right). The red dot is the setting we kept.

What we see. We tried 108 combinations in total. The curves are fairly flat at the start, so several settings perform almost equally well. This is a good sign: the result does not depend on one lucky setting. The best settings are listed below.

Model Past days used Best settings
LightGBM-Tweedie last 4 weeks learning_rate = 0.02, max_depth = 3, min_child_samples = 50, n_estimators = 200, tweedie_variance_power = 1.5
RandomForest last 4 weeks max_depth = 5, min_samples_leaf = 5, n_estimators = 300

5.3 Comparison on the validation period

Model MAE RMSE WAPE 30-day total error Score
LightGBM-Tweedie (tuned) 325 590 114.8% 26.5% 1.413
RandomForest (tuned) 368 605 130.1% 38.7% 1.688
Baseline: Weekday average of last 8 weeks 360 628 127.3% 42.3% 1.695
LightGBM with log-transformed sales 271 659 95.9% 83.2% 1.790
Baseline: Seasonal naive (same weekday last year) 479 992 169.4% 40.6% 2.099
How to read it. The bars show how far off each method was, on average, when predicting the total of a 30-day window. Grey bars are the simple baselines, the red bar is our best model. The table below gives all four error measures.

What we see. LightGBM-Tweedie is the best model and clearly beats both baselines. We also included one more variant on purpose: the same LightGBM trained on log-transformed sales, a common trick for skewed data. It looks good on daily errors (MAE 271), but it misses the 30-day total by about 83%. The reason is that the log transformation makes the model aim at a typical day and ignore the big orders, so it systematically forecasts too few bottles. This was an important lesson for us and the reason why our tuning score includes the 30-day total.

6 Feature selection and the role of the weather

6.1 Removing unhelpful features (RFECV)

More features are not always better. Features that carry no real information can make a model learn noise. We used recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV): the method trains the model, removes the least important feature, trains again, and repeats this. In the end it keeps the set of features with the lowest error over three time-ordered validation folds.

RFECV keeps 21 of 26 external features, including 12 of 12 weather features. Removed: dow_tue, dow_fri, is_holiday, pre_holiday, days_to_bbq_holiday.

At first sight this suggests that the weather is useful, because many weather features survive. But a feature can survive simply because it is correlated with the season, which the model would also know from the calendar. So we ran a more direct test.

6.2 With weather or without weather?

We trained the same tuned model three times, with three different feature sets, and compared them on the validation period and then on the test period:

  • calendar and holiday features only (no weather),
  • calendar plus all weather features,
  • the RFECV selection.
Model MAE RMSE WAPE 30-day total error Score
LightGBM-Tweedie: calendar + all weather 325 598 114.8% 27.4% 1.422
LightGBM-Tweedie: RFECV selection 325 598 114.8% 27.4% 1.422
LightGBM-Tweedie: calendar only (no weather) 320 599 112.9% 31.2% 1.442
Baseline: Weekday average of last 8 weeks 360 628 127.3% 42.3% 1.695
Baseline: Seasonal naive (same weekday last year) 479 992 169.4% 40.6% 2.099

On the validation period the best feature set is calendar + all weather (26 features). The three variants are very close to each other, which already hints that the weather does not change much.

7 Results on the test period

The test period (the last 180 days, January to July 2026) was never used for any decision so far. Here the model is retrained every 30 days with all data available up to that point and then forecasts the next 30 days. This is exactly how it would work in daily business.

Model MAE RMSE WAPE 30-day total error Score
LightGBM-Tweedie: calendar only (no weather) 474 865 102.6% 24.4% 1.270
LightGBM-Tweedie: calendar + all weather 475 867 102.7% 25.9% 1.286
LightGBM-Tweedie: RFECV selection 475 867 102.7% 25.9% 1.286
Baseline: Weekday average of last 8 weeks 516 888 111.6% 34.8% 1.465
Baseline: Seasonal naive (same weekday last year) 630 1153 136.2% 28.3% 1.644

Result. On data it has never seen, the model has a daily error (MAE) of 474 bottles, compared to 516 for the best simple baseline, an improvement of 8%. The 30-day total is missed by 24% on average, against 35% for that baseline.

7.1 Forecast against reality

How to read it. Top: every day of the test period. The grey line is what really happened, the red line is our forecast. Bottom: the same data added up per 30-day window, which is the number the business would plan with.

What we see. On the daily level the model does not try to guess the exact day of each large order. That is impossible from the data we have. Instead it predicts a realistic level for each weekday, which is why the red line looks smooth. On the 30-day level, which matters for planning, the forecast follows the real totals much better than the baseline. The largest miss is the window starting 30 Jun (-53%), where a few unusually large orders arrived. Over the six windows the average absolute miss is 26%.

7.2 Is the weather effect real?

To check whether the difference between the model with and without weather is real or just chance, we used a Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the daily errors of the two models. This test compares the two models day by day and does not assume normally distributed errors, which fits our skewed data.

Average daily error (test)
without weather 474 bottles
with weather 475 bottles
p-value 0.99

With p = 0.99 the difference is not statistically significant at the usual 5% level. In plain words: once the model knows the season and the weekday, the weather adds almost nothing.

7.3 Where does the model go wrong?

How to read it. Left: how often errors of each size occur. Positive values mean the model forecast too little. Right: the average size of the error on each weekday.

What we see. Most errors are small and close to zero. The long tail to the right comes from the large orders: on those days actual sales are far above the forecast. These misses are what drives the daily error measures up. Mondays have no error at all, because the model has correctly learned that nothing is sold on Mondays. The largest errors happen on the busy weekdays, where the big orders come in.

8 What drives the forecast?

To understand why the model makes its predictions, we used SHAP values. For every prediction, SHAP measures how much each feature pushed the forecast up or down compared to an average day. This turns the “black box” model into something we can explain.

How to read it. Each row is a feature, the most important at the top. Each dot is one day. Its colour shows whether the feature value was high (red) or low (blue) on that day, and its position shows whether it pushed the forecast up (right) or down (left).

What we see. The top features are the day of the week (especially Monday, where sales are always zero) and sales 7, 14 and 28 days ago. In other words, the model mainly learns the weekly rhythm and the recent level of business. Past sales and the calendar together explain 94% of the model’s decisions, while the weather features explain only 6%. This confirms the result of the statistical test.

9 The 30-day forecast

For the final forecast we retrain the chosen model on all available data. To show how uncertain the forecast is, we simulate 500 possible future paths. Each path adds errors that the model really made on the test period. From these paths we take an 80% range: in 8 out of 10 cases the real value should fall inside it.

How to read it. Grey: the last four months of real sales. Red line: the expected sales per day. Shaded area: the range in which daily sales will fall with 80% probability. The dashed line marks where the forecast starts.

What we see. For 30 July to 28 August 2026 we expect about 8,090 bottles, with an 80% range of 5,989 to 16,510. For comparison, the same period last year brought 8,959 bottles and the last 30 days brought 15,750. The drop compared to the last month is expected: the main BBQ season is over and sales usually fall in August. The upper end of the range is far above the forecast because a few very large orders could arrive, as happened in the past.

9.1 What if the summer is especially sunny?

We also tested a scenario with 30% more sunshine and 2 °C warmer weather than normal. The forecast changes to 8,153 bottles (+0.8%). Even a clearly better summer would barely change the expected sales, which again shows that the weather plays only a small role.

10 Conclusions and recommendations

1. The forecasting workflow works. We built a full pipeline from raw data to a 30-day forecast. On the test period our tuned LightGBM-Tweedie model beats the simple baselines (MAE 474 vs. 516 bottles per day) and predicts the 30-day total with an average error of 24%.

2. The weather adds almost no predictive power. Sunshine is related to sales at first sight, but this is mostly the season. With and without weather the model performs the same (p = 0.99), and weather features explain only 6% of the model’s decisions.

3. Sales are driven by large orders. 68% of all bottles are sold on the top 10% of days. Single days will always be hard to predict, but the 30-day total is reliable enough for planning.

4. The calendar is the strongest signal. The weekly rhythm (no sales on Mondays, little on Sundays) and the spring season from March to June explain most of the pattern.

10.0.1 Recommendations for the company

  • Plan stock around the season, not around the weather forecast. Production should be ramped up from February so that enough stock is available for the March to June peak.
  • Use the 30-day total and its range for planning. The upper end of the range shows how much safety stock is needed to cover a large unexpected order.
  • Collect better data on orders. Knowing which customer ordered, through which channel, and whether there was a promotion would help much more than more weather data, because the large orders are the main source of error.
  • Update the forecast every month. The model can be retrained with each new month of data in a few minutes.

10.0.2 Limitations

  • The weather data are national averages, so regional differences (for example a sunny south and a rainy north) are lost.
  • We have about 5.5 years of history, which means only five full seasons to learn from.
  • There is no information on prices, promotions or customers.
  • For the future, the weather is replaced by long-term averages.

10.0.3 Possible next steps

Further work could test additional models (for example models that predict whether a large order comes and how big it is separately), add promotion and customer data, and compare the forecast with the real sales once August 2026 is over.
